title: Capacity Estimation & Back-of-the-Envelope
summary: Turn "100M users" into QPS, terabytes, and gigabits in two minutes — the rough math that gives a system design its skeleton before you write a line of code.

blocks.markdown:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation sizes a system with rough math before you build it.

- Goal is the **order of magnitude**, not the exact figure — one server or a thousand?
- The chain is always **users → requests → QPS → storage / bandwidth / memory**.
- Use **powers of ten for counts** (users, requests) and **powers of two for bytes** (KB, MB, GB).
- Interviewers grade the **method and stated assumptions**, never the decimals.

blocks.subTitle: Which formula to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Each output has one formula. Memorize the four.

| Need | Formula |
|---|---|
| Request rate | daily requests ÷ ~100K sec |
| Disk size | writes/day × size × retention |
| Bandwidth | QPS × payload size |
| Cache / RAM | hot items × size each |

blocks.subTitle: The estimation chain
blocks.markdown:
Walk a fixed sequence; only the numbers change per problem.

![Estimation workflow from users to outputs](assets/capacity-estimation/estimation-workflow.svg)

- **State assumptions** — DAU, actions/user/day, read:write ratio, object size.
- **Daily requests** = DAU × actions, split by your ratio.
- **Average QPS** = daily requests ÷ seconds in a day.
- The top row is the input chain; storage, bandwidth, and memory each branch off the same traffic number.

assets.alt: Estimation workflow from users to outputs

blocks.subTitle: QPS and the peak factor
blocks.markdown:
Average QPS is daily requests over the seconds in a day — but everyone rounds.

![From daily users down to peak QPS](assets/capacity-estimation/traffic-funnel.svg)

- A day is **86,400 sec**, rounded to **~100,000** so dividing is instant (~15% error, acceptable).
- 1B requests/day ÷ 100K = **~10K QPS average**.
- Average is a lie for sizing — traffic clusters in waking hours. Multiply by a **peak factor of 2–3×**.
- 10K avg → **~30K peak QPS**, the number you actually provision for.

assets.alt: From daily users down to peak QPS

blocks.subTitle: Storage, bandwidth, memory
blocks.markdown:
Three outputs, three formulas — each one more multiply off the traffic number.

- **Storage** is cumulative: writes/day × bytes/write × retention. 100M records/day × 1 KB × 1 year ≈ **36 TB**. Add **×3 replication**.
- **Bandwidth** is a rate: read QPS × response size. 10K reads/s × 100 KB = **8 Gbps** — compare to a NIC's ~10–25 Gbps.
- **Memory** caches only the **hot set**, not everything: hot items × size each.
- Trick: each unit step (KB→MB→GB) is **×1000, or add 3 zeros**.

blocks.subTitle: Latency numbers to know
blocks.markdown:
Memorize the orders of magnitude — they tell you what's cheap and what bottlenecks.

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| Main memory (RAM) | ~100 ns |
| SSD random read | ~16 µs |
| Same-datacenter round trip | ~0.5 ms |
| HDD seek | ~10 ms |
| Cross-US round trip | ~150 ms |

The lesson: **RAM ~100× faster than SSD, SSD ~100× faster than disk**, and one cross-continent hop costs more than a million RAM reads. That's why we cache and avoid chatty cross-region calls.

blocks.subTitle: The judgment calls
blocks.markdown:
Estimation is cheap; the assumptions you bake in carry the judgment.

- **Precision vs speed** — round to one significant figure; the magnitude picks the architecture, decimals never do.
- **Average vs peak** — size for peak (2–3×) plus a safety margin, then autoscale rare spikes.
- **Read path vs write path** — read-heavy leans on caches and replicas; write-heavy on partitioning and write-optimized stores.
- **Storage vs compute vs bandwidth** — one runs out first. End every estimate with "this system is X-bound."

blocks.subTitle: Rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Quick heuristics that shape the design before you write any code.

- **Reads ≫ writes (≥10:1)** → cache and read replicas before sharding the primary.
- **Writes heavy or storage growing fast** → partition early, pick a write-optimized engine ([nosql-distributed-data](nosql-distributed-data)).
- **"One server can do it"** → stop; don't build distributed systems for 500 QPS.
- **Large objects (images, video)** → bandwidth and a CDN dominate, not QPS.
- **Always ×3 for replication** when turning raw bytes into provisioned storage.

blocks.subTitle: Worked example: feed service
blocks.markdown:
A Twitter-like feed, narrated. Round freely.

```text
DAU            = 100M
reads/user/day = 20      writes/user/day = 0.1
reads/day      = 2B      writes/day      = 10M
avg read QPS   = 2B/100K = 20K   write QPS = 100
peak (x3)      = 60K reads/s     300 writes/s
storage/5yr    = 10M*0.3KB*365*5 ~ 5.5 TB (x3 ~ 16 TB)
read bandwidth = 20K * 6KB = 120 MB/s ~ 1 Gbps
=> READ-BOUND: cache timelines, scale read replicas
```

- Writes and storage are **trivial**; the engineering goes into making 60K peak reads cheap.

blocks.subTitle: Worked example: photo storage
blocks.markdown:
Same user count, completely different bottleneck.

```text
DAU            = 100M
uploads/user/d = 2       views/user/d = 100
uploads/day    = 200M    views/day    = 10B
upload QPS     = 2K (peak 6K)
view QPS       = 100K (peak 300K)  -- mostly CDN
photo size     = 1.5 MB
storage/10yr   = 200M*1.5MB*365*10 ~ 1.1 EB (x1.5 EC ~ 1.6 EB)
read bandwidth = 100K * 1.5MB = 150 GB/s ~ 1.2 Tbps
=> STORAGE + BANDWIDTH-BOUND: object store + heavy CDN
```

- The feed is read-bound on small objects; this is storage- and bandwidth-bound on large ones.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems pick their own unit
blocks.markdown:
"Capacity" isn't always QPS — pick the unit that actually binds.

- **Twitter** — read:write in the hundreds-to-one drove fan-out-on-write; reads dominate, so make reads a cache lookup.
- **Amazon S3** — storage-bound; the dominant term is retention × replication, not request rate ([storage-systems](storage-systems)).
- **Netflix / YouTube** — bandwidth-bound; tens of millions of streams = terabits/sec, forcing edge CDNs.
- **WhatsApp** — bound by **concurrent persistent connections**, millions per box, not classic QPS.

The mistakes that sink an estimate:

- **Chasing accuracy.** Inputs are guesses, so false precision is meaningless — one significant figure suffices.
- **Sizing for average.** Carry the peak factor through, or the system dies at 9 a.m.
- **Confusing rate and total.** Bandwidth is bytes/sec; storage is bytes accumulated. Don't say "300 TB of bandwidth."
- **Forgetting replication.** Raw size isn't provisioned size — state your ×3 (or erasure-coding) multiplier.
- **The 1000× unit slip.** The #1 error: dropping or adding three zeros. Keep units on every number.
